title: GI & Nutrition Pharmacology — Session 1

summary.text: Acid-peptic disease is a **balance**: acid, pepsin, H. pylori and NSAIDs push against mucus, bicarbonate, prostaglandins and epithelial turnover.
Gastrin, histamine and acetylcholine converge on the **proton pump**: **H2 blockers** cut one input, **PPIs** block the final common pathway, **antacids** neutralize acid already made.
PPIs are the most potent but carry long-term risks — **B12 deficiency, hypomagnesemia, fractures, C. difficile** — and omeprazole blunts **clopidogrel** via CYP2C19.
**Sucralfate** shields the ulcer base (needs acid); **misoprostol** restores prostaglandins for NSAID-ulcer prevention but is **contraindicated in pregnancy**.
**H. pylori** needs eradication: triple therapy, or **bismuth quadruple** with penicillin allergy, recent macrolide, or clarithromycin resistance; test of cure ≥ 4 weeks later, off the PPI 2 weeks.

Antiemetics block one input to the vomiting center: **5-HT3** (ondansetron), **D2** (metoclopramide — boxed tardive dyskinesia), **NK1** (aprepitant), **H1/M1** (meclizine, scopolamine — motion sickness), plus **CB1** (dronabinol).

chunks.text: Acid-peptic disease is **a balance between mucosal defense and acid-driven aggression**.
**Aggressive factors:** gastric acid (HCl), pepsin, H. pylori infection, NSAID use (suppresses protective prostaglandins).
**Protective (mucosal defense) factors:** mucus–bicarbonate layer; prostaglandins (stimulate mucus/bicarbonate, maintain mucosal blood flow); epithelial cell turnover.
**GERD:** reflux of gastric contents into the esophagus, causing heartburn/regurgitation and, over time, esophageal mucosal injury.
**Peptic ulcer disease (PUD):** a break in the mucosa of the stomach or duodenum; most commonly caused by H. pylori infection or NSAID use.
**Gastritis:** inflammation of the gastric mucosa — acute (e.g., NSAID- or alcohol-related) or chronic (e.g., H. pylori-driven).
Over 90% of peptic ulcers are caused by H. pylori infection or NSAIDs; bile also counts as an aggressive factor.

Disease appears when aggressive factors win or defenses fall: aggressive factors (acid, pepsin, H. pylori, NSAIDs) overwhelm mucus, bicarbonate and prostaglandin-driven blood flow → mucosal injury → GERD, ulcer or gastritis.
**NSAIDs block COX-1 prostaglandins**, removing mucosal protection — the clearest example of tipping the balance.
**H. pylori urease makes ammonia**, which injures the mucosa.
**Stress and critical illness raise the risk of stress ulceration.**
**Gastrinoma (Zollinger-Ellison) causes severe acid hypersecretion.**
**Gastrin, histamine, and acetylcholine all converge on the parietal cell proton pump.** H2 blockers cut one input (histamine); PPIs block the last step itself.

**Physiology of acid secretion:** gastrin acts mainly by releasing histamine from ECL cells; acetylcholine (M3) stimulates the parietal cell directly; somatostatin from antral D cells turns gastrin off.
GERD, PUD and gastritis share the same drug toolkit: reduce acid, protect the mucosa, and/or eradicate H. pylori.
H. pylori and NSAIDs cause most PUD.
Figure 1 is the conceptual spine of the antisecretory section: be able to explain why PPIs are more complete acid suppressors than H2RAs from the diagram alone.
H2RAs block only the histamine input; gastrin and acetylcholine still drive the pump — PPIs block the final common pathway regardless of which input is active.
Aggressive: Gastric acid (HCl) · Protective: Mucus–bicarbonate layer
Aggressive: Pepsin · Protective: Prostaglandins (mucus, bicarbonate, mucosal blood flow)
Aggressive: H. pylori (urease → ammonia) · Protective: Epithelial cell turnover
Aggressive: NSAIDs (block COX-1 prostaglandins) · Protective: —
Why do NSAIDs cause ulcers? They block the COX-1 prostaglandins that make mucus and bicarbonate and keep mucosal blood flow up — they take the defense away.
Three keys, one lock: **gastrin, histamine, ACh** all turn the pump; PPIs change the lock.
Turning down acid production, or shielding the mucosa from it.
**Antacids** neutralize acid already made; **H2 blockers** block the histamine input; **PPIs** block the final common pathway — the most potent acid suppression.
Antacids are the oldest and most “patient-directed” class — a contrast to the receptor- and enzyme-targeted agents.
Omeprazole — PPI prototype (esomeprazole, pantoprazole, lansoprazole, dexlansoprazole).
Famotidine — most commonly used H2 blocker; cimetidine the CYP-inhibiting one.
Calcium carbonate, magnesium hydroxide, aluminum hydroxide — antacids.

**Antacids — mechanism: directly neutralize existing gastric acid (do not reduce acid production).** **Acid in stomach** → **antacid base (Al/Mg hydroxide, calcium carbonate) neutralizes H+** → **higher gastric pH** → rapid but short relief.

**H2RAs — mechanism: competitively block histamine at the H2 receptor on parietal cells.** Histamine from ECL cells → H2 receptor → cAMP rises → stimulates the proton pump; famotidine occupies the receptor competitively, so less acid.
**PPIs — mechanism: irreversibly inhibit the H⁺/K⁺-ATPase proton pump — the final common pathway of acid secretion.**
**PPI prodrug activated by acid** → **binds H⁺/K⁺ ATPase irreversibly** → **final step of acid secretion blocked**.

Pathway: enteric-coated prodrug absorbed in the small intestine → reaches the parietal cell canaliculus → activated by acid → binds a cysteine on H⁺/K⁺-ATPase covalently → **pump irreversibly blocked until new pumps are made**.
PPIs achieve substantially greater acid-suppression potency and longer duration of effect than H2RAs (Figure 4: potency 95 vs. 45; duration 90 vs. 50, illustrative).
H2 blockers inhibit 60–70% of 24-hour acid secretion; PPIs inhibit 90–98% because they block the final common pathway.
**Antacids:** onset is rapid, but duration is short — best for intermittent, mild symptom relief.
**H2RAs:** mild-to-moderate GERD, maintenance therapy, adjunct for peptic ulcer healing; best at controlling **nocturnal** acid.
**PPIs:** first-line for GERD, PUD healing, and H. pylori regimens.
Infrequent heartburn (fewer than three times per week): antacids or as-needed H2 blockers; antacids act faster but last 1–2 hours vs. 6–10 hours.
PPIs heal over 90% of duodenal ulcers within 4 weeks; GERD recurs in over 80% within 6 months of stopping.
Stress-related bleeding prophylaxis in high-risk ICU patients: an oral PPI if enteral meds are possible, otherwise IV H2 blocker or PPI.

**PPI long-term adverse effects: vitamin B12 deficiency, hypomagnesemia, increased fracture risk, and increased risk of Clostridioides difficile infection** — also pneumonia and acute interstitial nephritis.
**Abrupt PPI discontinuation after prolonged use can cause rebound acid hypersecretion.**

**Aluminum hydroxide — constipating. Magnesium hydroxide — can cause diarrhea; use caution in renal impairment (magnesium accumulation). Calcium carbonate — can cause constipation; risk of milk-alkali syndrome with excessive use.**
**Cimetidine:** antiandrogenic effects (gynecomastia) with prolonged use.
**Famotidine:** confusion risk in older adults with renal impairment.
**H2RAs: tolerance (tachyphylaxis) can develop with continuous use**, reducing effectiveness over time.
PPIs carry an FDA warning for hip, spine and wrist fractures and for life-threatening hypomagnesemia; 2–3-fold more C. difficile infection.
Sodium bicarbonate causes belching and metabolic alkalosis; excess calcium carbonate with dairy causes hypercalcemia, renal insufficiency and alkalosis (milk-alkali).
PPIs: contraindicated with rilpivirine (an HIV drug that needs stomach acid).
Magnesium and aluminum antacids are renally excreted: avoid long-term use in renal insufficiency.
**Antacids can impair absorption of many other oral drugs — separate dosing by at least 2 hours.** They bind levothyroxine, quinolones, tetracyclines, and iron.
**Omeprazole (a CYP2C19 inhibitor) can reduce clopidogrel activation, blunting its antiplatelet effect.** Omeprazole and esomeprazole both inhibit CYP2C19.
**Cimetidine is a potent CYP450 inhibitor (1A2, 2C19, 3A4)** — a callback to Lecture 1: it raises warfarin, phenytoin, and theophylline levels.
Famotidine has minimal CYP450 interaction.
Antacids should not be given within 2 hours of tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones, itraconazole, and iron.
With clopidogrel, prefer pantoprazole or rabeprazole (minimal CYP2C19 inhibition).
Less acid lowers absorption of ketoconazole, itraconazole, digoxin, and atazanavir.
**PPIs are best absorbed/effective when taken 30–60 minutes before a meal** (timed to peak pump activity) — they work best on actively secreting pumps.
CYP2C19 genotype alters PPI exposure; ultrarapid metabolizers may need higher doses.
Famotidine needs renal dose adjustment.
PPIs: food cuts bioavailability by about 50%; half-life about 1.5 hours yet acid inhibition lasts up to 24 hours; full effect takes 3–4 days.
PPIs need no renal dose reduction; consider reduction in severe liver impairment.
Many patients stay on PPIs far longer than necessary — the long-term adverse-effect list drives deprescribing conversations.
Ask: what happens to warfarin or phenytoin levels if cimetidine is added? They rise (CYP inhibition).
Name stems: **-prazole** PPIs (irreversibly block H+/K+ ATPase); **-tidine** H2 receptor antagonists (famotidine, ranitidine, cimetidine; competitively block the H2 receptor).

chunks.text: Why before breakfast? PPIs only hit pumps that are actively secreting; a meal switches pumps on, so the drug should be peaking when they turn on.
Why does PPI use cause B12 deficiency? Acid frees B12 from food protein; less acid, less B12 released.
Antacid bowel effects: **Al**uminum **al**ways constipates; **Mg** = **m**ore **g**oing (diarrhea).
Shielding the mucosa (sucralfate, misoprostol, bismuth) and treating the cause (H. pylori eradication).
**H. pylori is the leading identifiable cause of peptic ulcer disease — eradication, not just acid suppression, is the goal.**
Sucralfate — barrier over the ulcer base.
Misoprostol — PGE1 analog for NSAID-ulcer prevention.
Bismuth quadruple and PPI-based triple therapy for H. pylori.
**Sucralfate:** in acid (pH below 4) it polymerizes, binds the ulcer base and **forms a protective barrier**; requires an acidic environment to activate; minimal systemic absorption.
**Misoprostol:** **a prostaglandin E1 analog** — acts on EP receptors to reduce acid and increase mucus and bicarbonate, **restoring the protective prostaglandin tone that NSAIDs suppress**.
**Why H. pylori needs multiple drugs:** it lives in gastric mucus and buffers acid with urease-made ammonia.

A PPI raises gastric pH so bacteria enter a replicating state and antibiotics are more stable; amoxicillin blocks cell wall synthesis; clarithromycin (50S ribosome) or metronidazole adds a second antibiotic.
Sucralfate is sucrose complexed to sulfated aluminum hydroxide; less than 3% is absorbed.
Bismuth coats ulcers, has direct antimicrobial effects and binds enterotoxins (traveler’s diarrhea).
**Triple therapy:** PPI + amoxicillin + clarithromycin for 10–14 days (usual duration 14 days).

**Bismuth quadruple therapy:** PPI (or H2RA) + bismuth subsalicylate + metronidazole + tetracycline — preferred where clarithromycin resistance is a concern, with recent macrolide exposure, or with penicillin allergy.
**Penicillin allergy:** substitute metronidazole for amoxicillin in triple therapy.
Misoprostol is used specifically to prevent NSAID-induced ulcers.
Misoprostol cuts NSAID-induced ulcers to less than 3% and ulcer complications by 50%, but dosing 3–4 times daily and diarrhea limit use.
**Misoprostol: contraindicated in pregnancy — potent uterotonic/abortifacient effect** (boxed warning). Common adverse effects: diarrhea and cramping.
Sucralfate: constipation is common; aluminum accumulates in CKD.
Bismuth blackens stool (can mimic GI bleeding) and darkens the tongue; avoid in renal insufficiency.
Avoid tetracycline in pregnancy and in children.
Penicillin allergy rules out amoxicillin in H. pylori regimens.
**Separate sucralfate from other drugs by 2 hours** (give on an empty stomach, separated from antacids/PPIs).
**Clarithromycin inhibits CYP3A4** — must not be combined with simvastatin, lovastatin, or ergotamine.
**Metronidazole plus alcohol causes a disulfiram-like reaction.**
Sucralfate has minimal systemic absorption.
**Confirm eradication with testing (urea breath test or stool antigen) after completing therapy** — at least 4 weeks after, with the PPI held for 2 weeks (PPIs cause false negatives).
Counsel on completing a 10–14 day, 3–4 drug regimen — multi-drug regimens are a classic adherence problem.
After antibiotics, continue the PPI once daily for a total of 4–6 weeks to complete ulcer healing.
Case: confirmed H. pylori, penicillin allergy, and a macrolide two months ago. **Which eradication regimen is more appropriate for this patient, and why?**
Answer: bismuth quadruple therapy — recent macrolide exposure raises clarithromycin-resistance concern and the allergy rules out standard triple therapy.
Misoprostol’s pregnancy contraindication links to its other use (labor induction/medical abortion) — mechanism explains the contraindication.

Why is misoprostol forbidden in pregnancy? It is a prostaglandin — the same uterotonic effect that makes it a labor-induction drug.
Allergic to penicillin or recently on a macrolide? **Go Bismuth (quadruple)**.
**Four receptor systems feed one final common reflex.**

Four inputs converge on the **vomiting center in the medulla**: **gut and vagal (5-HT3)**, the **chemoreceptor trigger zone (D2, 5-HT3, NK1)**, the **vestibular (H1, M1)** system, and **higher cortical (anxiety, anticipatory)** input — benzodiazepines and cannabinoids.
**Motion sickness is vestibular** — H1/M1 blockers (meclizine, scopolamine) fit it.
Matching each drug to its input pathway (Figure 9) is the single most testable concept in this section.
Ondansetron — 5-HT3 antagonist.
Metoclopramide, prochlorperazine — D2 antagonists.
Aprepitant — NK1 antagonist.
Meclizine, scopolamine — H1/M1 antagonists.
Dronabinol, nabilone — cannabinoids (CB1).
**5-HT3 antagonists** block serotonin at gut vagal afferents/CTZ.

Chemotherapy or gut irritation damages enterochromaffin cells → serotonin binds 5-HT3 on vagal afferents and the CTZ → signal to the vomiting center; **ondansetron blocks 5-HT3, so no signal reaches the vomiting center**.
**D2 antagonists** block dopamine at the CTZ (metoclopramide, prochlorperazine).
**NK1 antagonists** block substance P/neurokinin at the CTZ (aprepitant).
**H1/M1 antagonists** block histamine/acetylcholine from the vestibular system (meclizine, scopolamine).

**Metoclopramide — mechanism: D2 antagonism (antiemetic effect) plus enhancement of upper-GI motility (prokinetic effect).** D2 blockade in the CTZ → less nausea; D2 blockade plus **5-HT4 agonism** in the gut → more acetylcholine → faster gastric emptying.
Dronabinol (CB1 agonist) crosses the blood-brain barrier and activates CB1 receptors in the vomiting center, CTZ and hypothalamus, reducing neurotransmitter release → less nausea, more appetite.
Mechanism is distinct from the four pathways (5-HT3, D2, NK1, H1/M1).
**Pathophysiology of vomiting:** the vomiting center sits in the lateral medullary reticular formation; the CTZ (area postrema) lies outside the blood-brain barrier.
Ondansetron: give before chemotherapy; oral ODT and IV forms are available.
**Metoclopramide clinical uses: nausea/vomiting and diabetic gastroparesis.**

**Dronabinol — a synthetic cannabinoid (CB1 receptor agonist) used for refractory chemotherapy-induced nausea/vomiting and appetite stimulation.** Typically reserved for patients who do not respond adequately to standard antiemetics.
**Chemotherapy:** combine classes with different targets — a 5-HT3 antagonist, an NK1 antagonist, and dexamethasone; avoid duplicating the same mechanism.
**Match drug to cause:** gut/vagal triggers respond to 5-HT3 antagonists; the CTZ to D2 or NK1 antagonists.
5-HT3 antagonists control vagal and chemotherapy emesis but poorly control motion sickness; palonosetron also prevents delayed emesis.
**Pharmacokinetics & pharmacodynamics (5-HT3):** first-generation agents have half-lives of 4–9 hours; palonosetron 40 hours; no dose cut in renal insufficiency.
NK1 antagonist + 5-HT3 antagonist + dexamethasone prevents acute emesis in 80–90% of highly emetogenic chemotherapy patients.
Benzodiazepines (lorazepam, diazepam) prevent anticipatory vomiting before chemotherapy.
Metoclopramide — **boxed warning: risk of tardive dyskinesia, particularly with prolonged use or high doses — limit duration of therapy.** Avoid beyond 12 weeks.
**Other extrapyramidal symptoms (acute dystonia, akathisia) can also occur**; acute dystonia is treated with diphenhydramine or benztropine.
**Ondansetron: QT prolongation** — caution with other QT-prolonging drugs and electrolyte problems. **Common effects: constipation, headache; serotonin syndrome risk with serotonergic drugs.**
**Cannabinoids: sedation, dizziness, mood/perception changes** (euphoria or dysphoria), tachycardia, orthostatic hypotension — counsel patients accordingly.
Metoclopramide: restlessness, drowsiness and agitation in 10–20%; extrapyramidal effects in 25% at high doses; prolactin rises (galactorrhea, gynecomastia).
Droperidol prolongs the QT interval (rare fatal torsades) — only if alternatives fail.
**Metoclopramide: contraindicated in GI obstruction; avoid in Parkinson disease.**
Ondansetron: serotonin syndrome risk with other serotonergic drugs; QT risk with other QT-prolonging drugs.
Cannabinoids: **additive CNS depression with sedatives and alcohol**.
Aprepitant is a CYP3A4 substrate/inhibitor: lowers INR with warfarin; dexamethasone dose is often reduced with it.
**CYP2D6 ultrarapid metabolizers may respond less well to ondansetron.**
**Metoclopramide: renal dosing needed; CYP2D6 poor metabolizers need lower doses** (higher exposure).
**Dronabinol is Schedule III; nabilone is Schedule II.** Use with caution in older adults.
Metoclopramide duration matters — many students remember only that it helps nausea.
Case: first-trimester nausea and vomiting not helped by dietary changes. **Which antiemetic class has the most established safety profile for use in this patient?**

Pyridoxine (vitamin B6), often with doxylamine, is typically first-line; ondansetron is commonly used too, though first-trimester data continue to evolve — weigh maternal benefit against fetal risk and consult current guidance.
Pyridoxine is a vitamin — a preview of Session 2’s vitamins and supplements.
Cannabinoid pharmacology is an expanding area in the newest Katzung edition.

1.title: GI & Nutrition Pharmacology
1.notes: Say: Today we follow two pathways. First, how the stomach makes acid and how we turn it down or protect the mucosa. Second, how the brain triggers vomiting and which receptor each antiemetic blocks.

2.title: Learning Objectives — Session 1
2.notes:
Orient students to the arc of this session: acid-peptic disease pathophysiology, antisecretory/mucosal-protective agents, H. pylori eradication, and antiemetics. This is the first of two sessions on GI & Nutrition Pharmacology — Session 2 picks up with lower-GI motility, IBD, and nutrition/dietary supplements on Nov 5.

Instructor script:

Objectives (2): Read them aloud. Then say: "Every drug today gets four answers: how it works, who it helps, what can go wrong, and what you tell the patient."

3.title: Required & Recommended Readings — Unit 3
3.notes:
Point students to the required and recommended texts for Unit 3 before diving into content. Katzung’s Chapters 62 and 65 are the required reading for this unit; Pharmacotherapy Principles and Practice is recommended as additional support, not a substitute.

Instructor script:

Readings (3): Point to Katzung and the course text. Everything on the slides is testable.

5.title: Mucosal Defense vs. Aggressive Factors
5.notes:
Everything in this section — GERD, PUD, gastritis — comes down to this balance tipping toward aggression or away from defense. NSAIDs are the clearest example: they tip the balance by suppressing the very prostaglandins that defend the mucosa.

Instructor script:

Say: Think of a balance. Acid, pepsin, H. pylori and NSAIDs push one way. Mucus, bicarbonate, prostaglandin-driven blood flow and epithelial turnover push back.

Know: Disease appears when aggressive factors win or defenses fall.

6.title: How Acid Injures the Mucosa
6.notes: Say: Walk the four boxes top to bottom. NSAIDs block COX-1 prostaglandins, so defenses fall. H. pylori makes urease and ammonia. Critical illness raises stress-ulcer risk. A gastrinoma drives extreme acid output.

7.title: GERD, Peptic Ulcer Disease, and Gastritis
7.notes:
These three diagnoses share the same drug toolkit — the therapeutic approach (reduce acid, protect mucosa, and/or eradicate H. pylori) is largely the same across all three.

Instructor script:

Say: Define each in one sentence. GERD is reflux of gastric contents into the esophagus. PUD is a break in the mucosa of the stomach or duodenum. Gastritis is mucosal inflammation.

Know: H. pylori and NSAIDs cause most PUD.

8.title: Gastric Acid Secretion: Where Antisecretory Drugs Act
8.notes:
This is the conceptual spine for the whole antisecretory-agent section that follows. Make sure students can explain WHY PPIs are more complete acid suppressors than H2RAs using this diagram alone.

Instructor script:

Say: Gastrin, histamine and acetylcholine all converge on the parietal cell proton pump. H2 blockers cut one input. PPIs block the last step.

9.notes:
Section transition.

Section 02: Antisecretory and mucosal-protective agents (slides 11-28).

10.title: Antacids
10.notes:
Antacids are the oldest and most "patient-directed" class here — good opening point to contrast with the receptor- and enzyme-targeted agents that follow.

Instructor script:

Say: They neutralize acid already made. They do not reduce acid production. Onset is fast and duration is short, so they suit mild, intermittent symptoms.

Know:

Aluminum constipates, magnesium causes diarrhea, calcium carbonate constipates and can cause milk-alkali syndrome with excess use.

They bind other drugs. Separate dosing by at least 2 hours.

11.title: H2 Receptor Antagonists
11.notes:
Cimetidine’s CYP450 inhibition is a great callback to Lecture 1’s drug-metabolism/interaction framework — ask students to predict what happens to warfarin or phenytoin levels if cimetidine is added.

Instructor script:

Know:

Tolerance (tachyphylaxis) develops with continued use.

Best at controlling nocturnal acid.

Famotidine needs renal dose adjustment and can cause confusion in older adults with renal impairment.

Cimetidine inhibits CYP450 (1A2, 2C19, 3A4) and has antiandrogenic effects, including gynecomastia.

12.title: H2 Blockers: Blocking the Histamine Signal
12.notes: Say: Histamine from the ECL cell binds the H2 receptor, cAMP rises, and the pump turns on. Famotidine competes at that receptor.

13.title: Proton Pump Inhibitors (PPIs)
13.notes:
The long-term adverse-effect list is high-yield for both exams and real-world deprescribing conversations — many patients are on PPIs far longer than clinically necessary.

Instructor script:

Know:

Take 30-60 minutes before the first meal, because PPIs work on actively secreting pumps.

Long-term risks: C. difficile infection, fractures, hypomagnesemia, B12 deficiency, pneumonia, acute interstitial nephritis, and rebound acid hypersecretion on stopping.

Omeprazole and esomeprazole inhibit CYP2C19 and can blunt clopidogrel activation.

CYP2C19 genotype changes PPI exposure. Ultrarapid metabo

14.title: PPIs: Irreversible Pump Inhibition
14.notes: Say: A PPI is an enteric-coated prodrug. It reaches the canaliculus, acid activates it, and it binds a cysteine on the H+/K+ ATPase covalently. The pump stays off until the cell makes new pumps.

15.title: PPIs vs. H2 Receptor Antagonists: Potency and Duration
15.notes:
This is the quantified version of the mechanistic point just made — more complete blockade (Figure 1) translates into both higher potency and longer duration here.

Instructor script:

Figure 4: Remind the class that the bars are illustrative relative values, not trial data. PPIs give greater and longer suppression than H2 blockers.

16.title: Mucosal Protective Agents
16.notes:
Misoprostol’s pregnancy contraindication is a must-know, high-stakes safety point — this is also the drug’s other well-known clinical use (labor induction/medical abortion), so the mechanism-to-contraindication link should feel obvious once stated.

Instructor script:

Know:

Sucralfate: separate from other drugs by 2 hours, aluminum accumulates in CKD, constipation is common.

Misoprostol: contraindicated in pregnancy because it causes uterine contractions. Diarrhea and cramping are common.

17.title: Sucralfate and Misoprostol: Strengthening Defense
17.notes: Say: Sucralfate polymerizes in acid, sticks to the ulcer base and forms a barrier. Misoprostol is a PGE1 analog. It acts on EP receptors to cut acid and raise mucus and bicarbonate.

18.title: Acid-Peptic Disease Agents at a Glance
18.notes:
Use this table as the organizing summary before moving into H. pylori eradication, which combines several of these agents together.

Instructor script:

Slide at a glance: Read across the table row by row. This is a good review point.

19.title: H. pylori Eradication Therapy
19.notes:
Multi-drug regimens like this are a classic source of adherence problems — worth pausing to ask students what patient-counseling points would most improve completion of a 10–14 day, 3–4 drug regimen.

Instructor script:

Know:

Usual duration is 14 days.

Bismuth quadruple therapy: PPI plus bismuth plus tetracycline plus metronidazole. It is preferred with penicillin allergy or prior macrolide exposure.

Confirm eradication at least 4 weeks after therapy and with the PPI held for 2 weeks.

Clarithromycin inhibits CYP3A4 (statins). Metronidazole plus alcohol causes a disulfiram-like reaction. A

20.title: Why H. pylori Needs Multiple Drugs
20.notes: Say: The goal is eradication, not only acid suppression. A PPI raises gastric pH, which makes antibiotics work better. Amoxicillin blocks the cell wall. Clarithromycin hits the 50S ribosome. Metronidazole adds another mechanism.

21.title: Choosing an H. pylori Regimen
21.notes:
This vignette forces students to apply two separate exclusion criteria at once — a good checkpoint for whether the regimen differences actually landed.

Instructor script:

Ask: "Penicillin allergy and a macrolide two months ago. Which regimen?" Answer: bismuth quadruple therapy.

22.title: Drug Names Reveal the Class: Acid-Peptic Disease
22.notes: Drug-name stems: -prazole is a PPI, -tidine is an H2 blocker, -prostol is a prostaglandin analog, -cillin is a penicillin, -thromycin is a macrolide. Sucralfate and bismuth subsalicylate have no stem.

24.title: Antiemetic Drug Classes
24.notes:
Each class corresponds to a different input feeding the vomiting center — the next slide shows these same four classes as a single mechanism diagram.

Instructor script:

Name the four target groups: 5-HT3, D2, NK1, and H1/M1.

25.title: Ondansetron: Blocking Serotonin at 5-HT3
25.notes:
Say: Chemotherapy injures enterochromaffin cells. They release serotonin. Serotonin binds 5-HT3 on vagal afferents and the chemoreceptor trigger zone. Ondansetron blocks that receptor.

Know:

Give before chemotherapy. Oral disintegrating and IV forms exist.

QT prolongation: caution with other QT-prolonging drugs and electrolyte problems.

Constipation and headache are common. Serotonin syndrome risk with other serotonergic drugs.

CYP2D6 ultrarapid metabolizers may respond less well.

26.title: Receptors in the Vomiting Pathway
26.notes:
Say: Four inputs reach the vomiting center in the medulla: the gut through the vagus, the trigger zone, the vestibular system and the cortex. Match the drug to the cause.

Know: For chemotherapy, combine drugs with different targets, such as a 5-HT3 antagonist, an NK1 antagonist and dexamethasone. Do not duplicate the same mechanism.

27.title: The Vomiting Reflex: Where Antiemetics Act
27.notes:
Have students match each generic drug name to its input pathway on this diagram before revealing the labels — this is the single most testable concept in the antiemetic section.

Instructor script:

Motion sickness is vestibular.

28.title: Metoclopramide: Antiemetic and Prokinetic
28.notes:
Metoclopramide’s boxed warning is one of the highest-yield patient-safety facts in this whole session — many students only remember "it helps nausea" without knowing why duration of use matters so much.

Instructor script:

Know:

Boxed warning: tardive dyskinesia. Avoid use beyond 12 weeks.

Acute dystonia is treated with diphenhydramine or benztropine.

Contraindicated in GI obstruction. Avoid in Parkinson disease.

Renal dose adjustment. CYP2D6 poor metabolizers have higher exposure.

29.title: Metoclopramide: D2 Blockade and 5-HT4 Agonism
29.notes: Say: D2 blockade in the trigger zone reduces nausea. In the gut, D2 blockade plus 5-HT4 agonism raises acetylcholine release and speeds gastric emptying.

30.title: Cannabinoids for Chemotherapy-Induced Nausea
30.notes:
This is a good moment to flag that cannabinoid pharmacology is an expanding area in the newest edition of Katzung — worth a brief mention that this mechanism class is distinct from everything else in this lecture.

Instructor script:

Know:

Reserved for patients who do not respond to standard antiemetics.

Dizziness, euphoria or dysphoria, tachycardia, orthostatic hypotension, additive CNS depression.

Use caution in older adults. Dronabinol is Schedule III and nabilone is Schedule II.

31.title: Cannabinoids: CB1 Activation in the Brain
31.notes: Say: Dronabinol and nabilone activate CB1 receptors in the vomiting center and trigger zone. They reduce neurotransmitter release. They also stimulate appetite.

32.title: Which Antiemetic for This Patient?
32.notes:
Use this to connect back to the Nutrition half of the unit (pyridoxine is a vitamin) — a preview of the Session 2 material on vitamins and supplements.

Instructor script:

First-trimester nausea unresponsive to diet. Let the class discuss. Pyridoxine (vitamin B6), often with doxylamine, is the usual first-line approach.

33.title: Drug Names Reveal the Class: Antiemetics
33.notes: Drug-name stems: -setron is a 5-HT3 antagonist, -pitant is an NK1 antagonist, -azine is a phenothiazine, -izine is an H1 antihistamine, -pramide is a benzamide D2 antagonist, -sone is a corticosteroid. Dronabinol, nabilone and scopolamine have no shared stem.

34.title: Session 1 Recap — To Be Continued
34.notes:
Close Session 1 by previewing Session 2 explicitly — students should leave knowing acid-peptic disease and antiemetics are complete, and that laxatives/antidiarrheals, IBD, and nutrition pick up first next time.

Instructor script:

Recap: Read the five points. Acid-peptic disease is a balance. PPIs block the final common pathway. H. pylori needs multiple drugs. Antiemetics follow receptor systems. Session 2 continues with lower-GI motility and nutrition.

36.title: Omeprazole (Prilosec)
36.notes:

Adverse effects: Headache, diarrhea, nausea; long-term: low B12 and Mg, fractures

U3-R1.question: Name the aggressive factors and the protective (mucosal defense) factors in acid-peptic disease.
U3-R1.answer: Aggressive — acid, pepsin, H. pylori, NSAIDs; protective — mucus-bicarbonate layer, prostaglandins, epithelial turnover.

U3-R2.question: Why do PPIs achieve more complete acid suppression than H2 receptor antagonists? What is the parietal cell's "final common pathway," and how does that explain the difference?
U3-R2.answer: PPIs block the H⁺/K⁺-ATPase itself, the final common pathway for gastrin/histamine/acetylcholine signals, so suppression occurs regardless of which input drives secretion; H2RAs block only histamine.

U3-R3.question: Name two long-term adverse effects of PPI use and explain the mechanism behind one of them.
U3-R3.answer: B12 deficiency, hypomagnesemia, fracture risk, C. difficile risk — e.g., reduced acid impairs B12 release from dietary protein.

U3-R4.question: What drug interaction makes omeprazole a concern in a patient taking clopidogrel after a cardiac stent?
U3-R4.answer: Omeprazole inhibits CYP2C19, blunting activation of the prodrug clopidogrel and its antiplatelet effect.

U3-R5.question: How do sucralfate and misoprostol protect the GI mucosa, and what is misoprostol's major contraindication?
U3-R5.answer: Sucralfate forms a barrier over the ulcer base (needs an acidic environment); misoprostol (PGE1 analog) restores prostaglandin tone NSAIDs suppress; contraindicated in pregnancy (abortifacient).

U3-R6.question: Name the two H. pylori eradication regimens discussed and the specific situation where bismuth quadruple therapy is preferred over standard triple therapy.
U3-R6.answer: Triple therapy (PPI+amoxicillin+clarithromycin) vs. bismuth quadruple therapy, preferred with clarithromycin-resistance concern, recent macrolide exposure, or penicillin allergy.

U3-R7.question: List the four antiemetic receptor targets covered and one representative drug for each. Which pathway is most relevant for motion sickness, and why?
U3-R7.answer: 5-HT3 — ondansetron; D2 — metoclopramide/prochlorperazine; NK1 — aprepitant; H1/M1 — meclizine/scopolamine (vestibular — relevant to motion sickness).

tree.name: Part 1 · Acid-Peptic Disease & Gastric Acid Secretion

children.name: Key definitions
facts: Acid-peptic disease is **a balance between mucosal defense and acid-driven aggression**.
**Aggressive factors:** gastric acid (HCl), pepsin, H. pylori infection, NSAID use (suppresses protective prostaglandins).
**Protective (mucosal defense) factors:** mucus–bicarbonate layer; prostaglandins (stimulate mucus/bicarbonate, maintain mucosal blood flow); epithelial cell turnover.
**GERD:** reflux of gastric contents into the esophagus, causing heartburn/regurgitation and, over time, esophageal mucosal injury.
**Peptic ulcer disease (PUD):** a break in the mucosa of the stomach or duodenum; most commonly caused by H. pylori infection or NSAID use.
**Gastritis:** inflammation of the gastric mucosa — acute (e.g., NSAID- or alcohol-related) or chronic (e.g., H. pylori-driven).
Over 90% of peptic ulcers are caused by H. pylori infection or NSAIDs; bile also counts as an aggressive factor.

children.name: How it works
facts: Disease appears when aggressive factors win or defenses fall: aggressive factors (acid, pepsin, H. pylori, NSAIDs) overwhelm mucus, bicarbonate and prostaglandin-driven blood flow → mucosal injury → GERD, ulcer or gastritis.
**NSAIDs block COX-1 prostaglandins**, removing mucosal protection — the clearest example of tipping the balance.
**H. pylori urease makes ammonia**, which injures the mucosa.
**Stress and critical illness raise the risk of stress ulceration.**
**Gastrinoma (Zollinger-Ellison) causes severe acid hypersecretion.**
**Gastrin, histamine, and acetylcholine all converge on the parietal cell proton pump.** H2 blockers cut one input (histamine); PPIs block the last step itself.

**Physiology of acid secretion:** gastrin acts mainly by releasing histamine from ECL cells; acetylcholine (M3) stimulates the parietal cell directly; somatostatin from antral D cells turns gastrin off.

children.name: Clinical relevance
facts: GERD, PUD and gastritis share the same drug toolkit: reduce acid, protect the mucosa, and/or eradicate H. pylori.
H. pylori and NSAIDs cause most PUD.

children.name: Drugs named as examples
facts: Figure 1 is the conceptual spine of the antisecretory section: be able to explain why PPIs are more complete acid suppressors than H2RAs from the diagram alone.

children.name: Exam traps
facts: H2RAs block only the histamine input; gastrin and acetylcholine still drive the pump — PPIs block the final common pathway regardless of which input is active.

tree.name: Part 2 · Antacids, H2 Blockers & Proton Pump Inhibitors

children.name: Class
facts: Turning down acid production, or shielding the mucosa from it.
**Antacids** neutralize acid already made; **H2 blockers** block the histamine input; **PPIs** block the final common pathway — the most potent acid suppression.
Antacids are the oldest and most “patient-directed” class — a contrast to the receptor- and enzyme-targeted agents.

children.name: Prototype + other drugs named
facts: Omeprazole — PPI prototype (esomeprazole, pantoprazole, lansoprazole, dexlansoprazole).
Famotidine — most commonly used H2 blocker; cimetidine the CYP-inhibiting one.
Calcium carbonate, magnesium hydroxide, aluminum hydroxide — antacids.

children.name: Mechanism of action
facts: **Antacids — mechanism: directly neutralize existing gastric acid (do not reduce acid production).** **Acid in stomach** → **antacid base (Al/Mg hydroxide, calcium carbonate) neutralizes H+** → **higher gastric pH** → rapid but short relief.

**H2RAs — mechanism: competitively block histamine at the H2 receptor on parietal cells.** Histamine from ECL cells → H2 receptor → cAMP rises → stimulates the proton pump; famotidine occupies the receptor competitively, so less acid.
**PPIs — mechanism: irreversibly inhibit the H⁺/K⁺-ATPase proton pump — the final common pathway of acid secretion.**
**PPI prodrug activated by acid** → **binds H⁺/K⁺ ATPase irreversibly** → **final step of acid secretion blocked**.

Pathway: enteric-coated prodrug absorbed in the small intestine → reaches the parietal cell canaliculus → activated by acid → binds a cysteine on H⁺/K⁺-ATPase covalently → **pump irreversibly blocked until new pumps are made**.
PPIs achieve substantially greater acid-suppression potency and longer duration of effect than H2RAs (Figure 4: potency 95 vs. 45; duration 90 vs. 50, illustrative).
H2 blockers inhibit 60–70% of 24-hour acid secretion; PPIs inhibit 90–98% because they block the final common pathway.

children.name: Indications
facts: **Antacids:** onset is rapid, but duration is short — best for intermittent, mild symptom relief.
**H2RAs:** mild-to-moderate GERD, maintenance therapy, adjunct for peptic ulcer healing; best at controlling **nocturnal** acid.
**PPIs:** first-line for GERD, PUD healing, and H. pylori regimens.
Infrequent heartburn (fewer than three times per week): antacids or as-needed H2 blockers; antacids act faster but last 1–2 hours vs. 6–10 hours.
PPIs heal over 90% of duodenal ulcers within 4 weeks; GERD recurs in over 80% within 6 months of stopping.
Stress-related bleeding prophylaxis in high-risk ICU patients: an oral PPI if enteral meds are possible, otherwise IV H2 blocker or PPI.

children.name: Adverse effects (boxed warnings first)
facts: **PPI long-term adverse effects: vitamin B12 deficiency, hypomagnesemia, increased fracture risk, and increased risk of Clostridioides difficile infection** — also pneumonia and acute interstitial nephritis.
**Abrupt PPI discontinuation after prolonged use can cause rebound acid hypersecretion.**

**Aluminum hydroxide — constipating. Magnesium hydroxide — can cause diarrhea; use caution in renal impairment (magnesium accumulation). Calcium carbonate — can cause constipation; risk of milk-alkali syndrome with excessive use.**
**Cimetidine:** antiandrogenic effects (gynecomastia) with prolonged use.
**Famotidine:** confusion risk in older adults with renal impairment.
**H2RAs: tolerance (tachyphylaxis) can develop with continuous use**, reducing effectiveness over time.
PPIs carry an FDA warning for hip, spine and wrist fractures and for life-threatening hypomagnesemia; 2–3-fold more C. difficile infection.
Sodium bicarbonate causes belching and metabolic alkalosis; excess calcium carbonate with dairy causes hypercalcemia, renal insufficiency and alkalosis (milk-alkali).

children.name: Contraindications
facts: PPIs: contraindicated with rilpivirine (an HIV drug that needs stomach acid).
Magnesium and aluminum antacids are renally excreted: avoid long-term use in renal insufficiency.

children.name: Drug interactions
facts: **Antacids can impair absorption of many other oral drugs — separate dosing by at least 2 hours.** They bind levothyroxine, quinolones, tetracyclines, and iron.
**Omeprazole (a CYP2C19 inhibitor) can reduce clopidogrel activation, blunting its antiplatelet effect.** Omeprazole and esomeprazole both inhibit CYP2C19.
**Cimetidine is a potent CYP450 inhibitor (1A2, 2C19, 3A4)** — a callback to Lecture 1: it raises warfarin, phenytoin, and theophylline levels.
Famotidine has minimal CYP450 interaction.
Antacids should not be given within 2 hours of tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones, itraconazole, and iron.
With clopidogrel, prefer pantoprazole or rabeprazole (minimal CYP2C19 inhibition).
Less acid lowers absorption of ketoconazole, itraconazole, digoxin, and atazanavir.

children.name: Pharmacokinetics
facts: **PPIs are best absorbed/effective when taken 30–60 minutes before a meal** (timed to peak pump activity) — they work best on actively secreting pumps.
CYP2C19 genotype alters PPI exposure; ultrarapid metabolizers may need higher doses.
Famotidine needs renal dose adjustment.
PPIs: food cuts bioavailability by about 50%; half-life about 1.5 hours yet acid inhibition lasts up to 24 hours; full effect takes 3–4 days.
PPIs need no renal dose reduction; consider reduction in severe liver impairment.

children.name: Monitoring
facts: Many patients stay on PPIs far longer than necessary — the long-term adverse-effect list drives deprescribing conversations.

children.name: Clinical pearls / "why" hook
facts: Ask: what happens to warfarin or phenytoin levels if cimetidine is added? They rise (CYP inhibition).
Name stems: **-prazole** PPIs (irreversibly block H+/K+ ATPase); **-tidine** H2 receptor antagonists (famotidine, ranitidine, cimetidine; competitively block the H2 receptor).

tree.name: Part 3 · Mucosal Protectants & H. pylori Eradication

children.name: Class
facts: Shielding the mucosa (sucralfate, misoprostol, bismuth) and treating the cause (H. pylori eradication).
**H. pylori is the leading identifiable cause of peptic ulcer disease — eradication, not just acid suppression, is the goal.**

children.name: Prototype + other drugs named
facts: Sucralfate — barrier over the ulcer base.
Misoprostol — PGE1 analog for NSAID-ulcer prevention.
Bismuth quadruple and PPI-based triple therapy for H. pylori.

children.name: Mechanism of action
facts: **Sucralfate:** in acid (pH below 4) it polymerizes, binds the ulcer base and **forms a protective barrier**; requires an acidic environment to activate; minimal systemic absorption.
**Misoprostol:** **a prostaglandin E1 analog** — acts on EP receptors to reduce acid and increase mucus and bicarbonate, **restoring the protective prostaglandin tone that NSAIDs suppress**.
**Why H. pylori needs multiple drugs:** it lives in gastric mucus and buffers acid with urease-made ammonia.

A PPI raises gastric pH so bacteria enter a replicating state and antibiotics are more stable; amoxicillin blocks cell wall synthesis; clarithromycin (50S ribosome) or metronidazole adds a second antibiotic.
Sucralfate is sucrose complexed to sulfated aluminum hydroxide; less than 3% is absorbed.
Bismuth coats ulcers, has direct antimicrobial effects and binds enterotoxins (traveler’s diarrhea).

children.name: Indications
facts: **Triple therapy:** PPI + amoxicillin + clarithromycin for 10–14 days (usual duration 14 days).

**Bismuth quadruple therapy:** PPI (or H2RA) + bismuth subsalicylate + metronidazole + tetracycline — preferred where clarithromycin resistance is a concern, with recent macrolide exposure, or with penicillin allergy.
**Penicillin allergy:** substitute metronidazole for amoxicillin in triple therapy.
Misoprostol is used specifically to prevent NSAID-induced ulcers.
Misoprostol cuts NSAID-induced ulcers to less than 3% and ulcer complications by 50%, but dosing 3–4 times daily and diarrhea limit use.

children.name: Adverse effects (boxed warnings first)
facts: **Misoprostol: contraindicated in pregnancy — potent uterotonic/abortifacient effect** (boxed warning). Common adverse effects: diarrhea and cramping.
Sucralfate: constipation is common; aluminum accumulates in CKD.
Bismuth blackens stool (can mimic GI bleeding) and darkens the tongue; avoid in renal insufficiency.

children.name: Contraindications
facts: Avoid tetracycline in pregnancy and in children.
Penicillin allergy rules out amoxicillin in H. pylori regimens.

children.name: Drug interactions
facts: **Separate sucralfate from other drugs by 2 hours** (give on an empty stomach, separated from antacids/PPIs).
**Clarithromycin inhibits CYP3A4** — must not be combined with simvastatin, lovastatin, or ergotamine.
**Metronidazole plus alcohol causes a disulfiram-like reaction.**

children.name: Pharmacokinetics
facts: Sucralfate has minimal systemic absorption.

children.name: Monitoring
facts: **Confirm eradication with testing (urea breath test or stool antigen) after completing therapy** — at least 4 weeks after, with the PPI held for 2 weeks (PPIs cause false negatives).
Counsel on completing a 10–14 day, 3–4 drug regimen — multi-drug regimens are a classic adherence problem.
After antibiotics, continue the PPI once daily for a total of 4–6 weeks to complete ulcer healing.

children.name: Clinical pearls / "why" hook
facts: Case: confirmed H. pylori, penicillin allergy, and a macrolide two months ago. **Which eradication regimen is more appropriate for this patient, and why?**
Answer: bismuth quadruple therapy — recent macrolide exposure raises clarithromycin-resistance concern and the allergy rules out standard triple therapy.
Misoprostol’s pregnancy contraindication links to its other use (labor induction/medical abortion) — mechanism explains the contraindication.

Name stems: **-prostol** prostaglandin analogs (misoprostol); **-cillin** penicillins (amoxicillin; blocks cell wall synthesis); **-thromycin** macrolides (clarithromycin; -mycin alone is not reliable, e.g., gentamicin); sucralfate and bismuth subsalicylate share no stem.

children.name: Class
facts: **Four receptor systems feed one final common reflex.**

Four inputs converge on the **vomiting center in the medulla**: **gut and vagal (5-HT3)**, the **chemoreceptor trigger zone (D2, 5-HT3, NK1)**, the **vestibular (H1, M1)** system, and **higher cortical (anxiety, anticipatory)** input — benzodiazepines and cannabinoids.
**Motion sickness is vestibular** — H1/M1 blockers (meclizine, scopolamine) fit it.
Matching each drug to its input pathway (Figure 9) is the single most testable concept in this section.

children.name: Prototype + other drugs named
facts: Ondansetron — 5-HT3 antagonist.
Metoclopramide, prochlorperazine — D2 antagonists.
Aprepitant — NK1 antagonist.
Meclizine, scopolamine — H1/M1 antagonists.
Dronabinol, nabilone — cannabinoids (CB1).

children.name: Mechanism of action
facts: **5-HT3 antagonists** block serotonin at gut vagal afferents/CTZ.

Chemotherapy or gut irritation damages enterochromaffin cells → serotonin binds 5-HT3 on vagal afferents and the CTZ → signal to the vomiting center; **ondansetron blocks 5-HT3, so no signal reaches the vomiting center**.
**D2 antagonists** block dopamine at the CTZ (metoclopramide, prochlorperazine).
**NK1 antagonists** block substance P/neurokinin at the CTZ (aprepitant).
**H1/M1 antagonists** block histamine/acetylcholine from the vestibular system (meclizine, scopolamine).

**Metoclopramide — mechanism: D2 antagonism (antiemetic effect) plus enhancement of upper-GI motility (prokinetic effect).** D2 blockade in the CTZ → less nausea; D2 blockade plus **5-HT4 agonism** in the gut → more acetylcholine → faster gastric emptying.
Dronabinol (CB1 agonist) crosses the blood-brain barrier and activates CB1 receptors in the vomiting center, CTZ and hypothalamus, reducing neurotransmitter release → less nausea, more appetite.
Mechanism is distinct from the four pathways (5-HT3, D2, NK1, H1/M1).
**Pathophysiology of vomiting:** the vomiting center sits in the lateral medullary reticular formation; the CTZ (area postrema) lies outside the blood-brain barrier.

children.name: Indications
facts: Ondansetron: give before chemotherapy; oral ODT and IV forms are available.
**Metoclopramide clinical uses: nausea/vomiting and diabetic gastroparesis.**

**Dronabinol — a synthetic cannabinoid (CB1 receptor agonist) used for refractory chemotherapy-induced nausea/vomiting and appetite stimulation.** Typically reserved for patients who do not respond adequately to standard antiemetics.
**Chemotherapy:** combine classes with different targets — a 5-HT3 antagonist, an NK1 antagonist, and dexamethasone; avoid duplicating the same mechanism.
**Match drug to cause:** gut/vagal triggers respond to 5-HT3 antagonists; the CTZ to D2 or NK1 antagonists.
5-HT3 antagonists control vagal and chemotherapy emesis but poorly control motion sickness; palonosetron also prevents delayed emesis.
**Pharmacokinetics & pharmacodynamics (5-HT3):** first-generation agents have half-lives of 4–9 hours; palonosetron 40 hours; no dose cut in renal insufficiency.
NK1 antagonist + 5-HT3 antagonist + dexamethasone prevents acute emesis in 80–90% of highly emetogenic chemotherapy patients.
Benzodiazepines (lorazepam, diazepam) prevent anticipatory vomiting before chemotherapy.

children.name: Adverse effects (boxed warnings first)
facts: Metoclopramide — **boxed warning: risk of tardive dyskinesia, particularly with prolonged use or high doses — limit duration of therapy.** Avoid beyond 12 weeks.
**Other extrapyramidal symptoms (acute dystonia, akathisia) can also occur**; acute dystonia is treated with diphenhydramine or benztropine.
**Ondansetron: QT prolongation** — caution with other QT-prolonging drugs and electrolyte problems. **Common effects: constipation, headache; serotonin syndrome risk with serotonergic drugs.**
**Cannabinoids: sedation, dizziness, mood/perception changes** (euphoria or dysphoria), tachycardia, orthostatic hypotension — counsel patients accordingly.
Metoclopramide: restlessness, drowsiness and agitation in 10–20%; extrapyramidal effects in 25% at high doses; prolactin rises (galactorrhea, gynecomastia).
Droperidol prolongs the QT interval (rare fatal torsades) — only if alternatives fail.

children.name: Contraindications
facts: **Metoclopramide: contraindicated in GI obstruction; avoid in Parkinson disease.**

children.name: Drug interactions
facts: Ondansetron: serotonin syndrome risk with other serotonergic drugs; QT risk with other QT-prolonging drugs.
Cannabinoids: **additive CNS depression with sedatives and alcohol**.
Aprepitant is a CYP3A4 substrate/inhibitor: lowers INR with warfarin; dexamethasone dose is often reduced with it.

children.name: Pharmacokinetics
facts: **CYP2D6 ultrarapid metabolizers may respond less well to ondansetron.**
**Metoclopramide: renal dosing needed; CYP2D6 poor metabolizers need lower doses** (higher exposure).

children.name: Monitoring
facts: **Dronabinol is Schedule III; nabilone is Schedule II.** Use with caution in older adults.
Metoclopramide duration matters — many students remember only that it helps nausea.

children.name: Clinical pearls / "why" hook
facts: Case: first-trimester nausea and vomiting not helped by dietary changes. **Which antiemetic class has the most established safety profile for use in this patient?**

Pyridoxine (vitamin B6), often with doxylamine, is typically first-line; ondansetron is commonly used too, though first-trimester data continue to evolve — weigh maternal benefit against fetal risk and consult current guidance.
Pyridoxine is a vitamin — a preview of Session 2’s vitamins and supplements.
Cannabinoid pharmacology is an expanding area in the newest Katzung edition.

brief.part: Part 1 · Acid-Peptic Disease & Gastric Acid Secretion
hy: Acid-peptic disease reflects an imbalance between mucosal defense and aggressive factors (acid, pepsin, H. pylori, NSAIDs).
H. pylori and NSAIDs cause most PUD.
traps: H2RAs block only the histamine input; gastrin and acetylcholine still drive the pump — PPIs block the final common pathway regardless of which input is active.

brief.part: Part 2 · Antacids, H2 Blockers & Proton Pump Inhibitors
hy: PPIs block the parietal cell’s final common pathway and are the most potent antisecretory agents, but carry real long-term risks (B12 deficiency, hypomagnesemia, fracture, C. difficile).
Antacids: fast, short, don’t reduce production; separate other drugs by 2 hours.
Cimetidine: CYP inhibitor + gynecomastia; famotidine: renal dosing, minimal CYP.
Omeprazole + clopidogrel: CYP2C19 inhibition blunts activation.

brief.part: Part 3 · Mucosal Protectants & H. pylori Eradication
hy: H. pylori eradication requires multi-drug regimens (triple or bismuth quadruple therapy), not acid suppression alone.
Misoprostol: PGE1 analog, NSAID-ulcer prevention, never in pregnancy.
Sucralfate needs acid; separate from other drugs by 2 hours.
Antiemetics are organized by the receptor pathway they block — serotonin (5-HT3), dopamine/neurokinin (CTZ), or histamine/acetylcholine (vestibular) — all converging on the vomiting center.
Metoclopramide: boxed tardive dyskinesia; avoid beyond 12 weeks.
Ondansetron: QT prolongation; give before chemo.
